_comment: Empirical grounding layer. Every detector type is traced to its real-world bug class (CWE), its real-world signature, the chains it composes into (cross-ref chains.json), citable references, per-class bypass techniques, and the high-value assets (crown jewels) that class typically hits. Detection is derived from this data, never hardcoded. References are public standards (CWE/OWASP) and disclosed-report classes — no vendor/product framing.

patterns.name: SQL Injection
patterns.real_world: User input is interpolated into a SQL query by string concatenation instead of parameterization. The single most-reported web class; real disclosures range from boolean/UNION extraction to stacked queries for admin takeover.
detection_signatures: raw string-interpolated query into a SQL sink
cross-file: concatenated variable with no visible source
bypass_techniques: comment/whitespace obfuscation to slip past keyword filters
second-order: store payload, trigger on a later read
time-based blind when output is suppressed

patterns.name: Server-Side Request Forgery
patterns.real_world: A server fetches an attacker-supplied URL with no host allowlist, letting it reach cloud metadata endpoints, internal services, or the loopback interface.
detection_signatures: server-side fetch of a request-controlled URL
bypass_techniques: DNS rebinding to pass host checks
redirect chains to a blocklisted host

patterns.name: Server-Side Template Injection
patterns.real_world: User input reaches a template engine (Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, ERB, …) that evaluates expressions, yielding code execution via template syntax like {{7*7}}.
detection_signatures: expression evaluation in a template engine
bypass_techniques: unicode/alternate delimiter to dodge input filters

patterns.name: XML External Entity Injection
patterns.real_world: An XML parser resolves external entities, letting an attacker read local files or hit internal URLs via DOCTYPE entity definitions.
detection_signatures: XML parse without disabling external entities
bypass_techniques: parameter entities + external DTD for blind exfiltration
UTF-7/UTF-16 encodings to dodge ASCII filters
crown_jewels: cloud metadata via file:// + SSRF chain

patterns.name: Insecure Deserialization
patterns.real_world: Attacker-controlled serialized data is deserialized and escalated through a magic-method gadget chain (__destruct/__wakeup/__toString) into code execution or object injection.
references: OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures
bypass_techniques: custom gadget chains for the app's own classes
phar:// stream wrappers to trigger unserialize
encrypted-session forgery once a secret leaks

patterns.name: PHP Type Juggling (Loose Comparison)
patterns.real_world: A loose comparison (==) between user input and a hash/secret collapses via the 0e magic-hash or numeric-string coercion, bypassing authentication.
detection_signatures: loose comparison == of user input against a secret/hash
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

patterns.name: Mass Assignment
patterns.real_world: Request data is bound to model fields without an allowlist (extract()/parse_str/framework mass-assign), letting an attacker set privileged fields like role or is_admin.
detection_signatures: extract()/parse_str of request data without a safe flag
references: OWASP API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
bypass_techniques: nested/array parameters to reach guarded fields
adding is_admin/role/verified fields to a request

patterns.name: Prototype Pollution
patterns.real_world: A deep merge of request data into an object pollutes Object.prototype, corrupting logic and escalating to code execution in gadget-heavy runtimes.
detection_signatures: deep merge/extend of request data into objects
bypass_techniques: array-key pollution to reach the merge

patterns.name: CRLF Injection / Header Injection
patterns.real_world: Request-controlled newlines are written into an HTTP header, enabling response splitting, cookie injection, or cache poisoning.
detection_signatures: request input reaches a header without CR/LF stripping

patterns.name: Path Traversal / Path Confusion
patterns.real_world: A request-controlled path is normalized or resolved without confinement (../, %2e%2e, absolute paths), reading or writing files outside the intended directory.
detection_signatures: request input reaches a file path without confinement
bypass_techniques: log-poisoning to turn LFI into RCE
crown_jewels: writable dirs for a shell drop

patterns.name: Wrong-Context Sanitization
patterns.real_world: A value is sanitized for one context (e.g. HTML) but reaches a sink that needs a different context (e.g. SQL), so the sanitizer provides no real protection.
detection_signatures: a sanitizer/validator for context X feeding a sink that requires context Y
bypass_techniques: context mismatch (HTML-escape then SQL, or vice-versa)
double encoding to survive a single decode
crown_jewels: stored data that re-enters a different sink

patterns.name: Missing Authorization (Broken Access Control)
patterns.real_world: A state-changing handler lacks a capability/ownership check, letting an unauthenticated or low-privilege caller perform an admin action.
detection_signatures: state-changing operation with no current_user_can/is_user_logged_in check
bypass_techniques: HTTP verb tampering (GET vs POST vs PUT)
validation: Two-account test: attacker account A reads victim account B's object (A's token + B's id -> B's data). A single self-account test does not prove IDOR.

patterns.name: Missing Nonce (CSRF)
patterns.real_world: A state-changing action lacks an anti-CSRF token, letting a victim's browser perform the action on their behalf via a forged request.
detection_signatures: state-changing operation with no nonce/referer verification
bypass_techniques: verb switching to skip the check

patterns.name: Unrestricted File Upload
patterns.real_world: A file is uploaded with an attacker-controlled name/extension and no server-side filetype whitelist, landing web-reachable for code execution.
crown_jewels: document converters (PDF/Office) with a known chain

patterns.name: Privilege Escalation
patterns.real_world: A role/capability/user change is fed by request input and reachable from a public entry point with no capability check, letting a user self-assign admin.
detection_signatures: cross-file: sink reachable from public hook with no capability check
bypass_techniques: missing capability check on a public hook

patterns.name: Hardcoded Credentials
patterns.real_world: A secret (API key, database password, access token, private key) is committed in source, exposing it to anyone with repo access. Real disclosures regularly turn a leaked key into account takeover or cloud compromise.
detection_signatures: high-entropy token under a non-obvious name
bypass_techniques: base64/hex-encoded secrets that evade naive regex

patterns.name: LLM Prompt Injection
patterns.real_world: Untrusted text reaches an LLM call (chat/completion/invoke) without a prompt-injection boundary, letting the input override instructions, leak the system prompt, or steer the model into a privileged action.
detection_signatures: an LLM provider call (openai/anthropic/langchain/llm) with request input in scope
no visible system-prompt boundary or output filtering
bypass_techniques: delimiter/role confusion to escape the system prompt
context overflow to displace earlier constraints
crown_jewels: privileged actions (email/send/pay) gated on model output
validation: RUN-TWICE RULE — the extraction/injection must reproduce token-for-token across two fresh sessions (filter out model confabulation)
NON-GUESSABLE ANCHOR — it must leak an actual verifiable internal key, endpoint URL, or cross-tenant data, not a plausible guess
OOB PROOF — tool-use or markdown exfiltration must produce a verifiable callback log on your listener

patterns.name: GraphQL Introspection / Playground Exposure
patterns.real_world: GraphQL introspection or a playground is left enabled in production, exposing the full schema (every query/mutation/field) and enabling interactive querying for recon.
detection_signatures: introspection/playground/graphiql set true in a production-reachable config
bypass_techniques: alternate introspection queries when the standard one is blocked
field suggestion / error messages leaking the schema

patterns.name: OAuth Redirect URI Misconfiguration
patterns.real_world: An OAuth redirect_uri/callback is fed by request input with no static allowlist, letting an attacker redirect the authorization code or token to an attacker-controlled endpoint.
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures
bypass_techniques: OAuth mix-up between IdP and client

patterns.name: gRPC Reflection Exposed
patterns.real_world: gRPC server reflection is enabled, enumerating every service and method to any caller and leaking the API contract.
bypass_techniques: proto extraction to reconstruct the contract

patterns.real_world: Attacker publishes an internal package name (e.g. company-utils) on the public registry with a higher version; the build resolves it and pulls malicious code into CI/deploy.
detection_signatures: --index-url / --extra-index-url pointing at a public registry (pypi.org/npmjs.org/rubygems.org) in a manifest or build file
a scoped package (@company/pkg) referenced with no private registry pinned
bypass_techniques: scoped-name squatting (npm @scope is not reserved unless registered)
version pinning (>=0.0.1) so a higher attacker version wins
PEP 503 private-index fallback to public PyPI
crown_jewels: artifact/deploy credentials baked into the build
the internal package name registry (what to squat)

patterns.real_world: A poisoned model file (pickle) hosted at a URL or uploaded by a user is loaded via torch.load/joblib.load without the safe flag → arbitrary code execution on load.
detection_signatures: joblib.load(...) / keras.models.load_model(...) / np.load(...allow_pickle=True) on an untrusted path/URL
bypass_techniques: model file masquerading as a benign artifact (weights.pt with a pickle payload)
indirect load: download via URL then load locally

patterns.real_world: A Rust library uses std::mem::transmute to reinterpret an attacker-influenced value as a reference, or builds a slice via from_raw_parts with a caller-supplied length, producing out-of-bounds access / use-after-free inside an unsafe block.
references: Rust Foundation — Unsafe Rust in the Wild
bypass_techniques: transmute to a larger/smaller layout to defeat the borrow checker
unsafe + raw pointer arithmetic past the bounds
FFI (extern C) without validating C-side lengths
crown_jewels: the unsafe block's invariants (what must hold for soundness)

patterns.real_world: A server logs or prints a user-supplied string as the format argument — println!(user_input) — so the attacker's format specifiers (positional args, width/precision) read or corrupt memory.
detection_signatures: format!(var) / println!(var) / print!(var) / eprintln!(var) with a VARIABLE as the format string (not a literal)
bypass_techniques: width/precision specifiers to read past the intended argument
positional args ({0} {1} ...) to reach unintended arguments
indirect format via a helper that passes user input straight into format!
crown_jewels: the formatting arguments on the stack
any panic path that formats attacker input

patterns.name: JWT Algorithm Confusion (RS256 -> HS256)
patterns.signature: alg-dispatch verifier accepting RS256 AND HS256 with public/shared HMAC key
patterns.real_world: A hand-written JWT verifier dispatches on the token's alg header and accepts BOTH RS256 (asymmetric) and HS256 (symmetric HMAC), with the HS256 secret derived from the RSA public key. Setting alg=HS256 and signing with the public key forges a valid token.
detection_signatures: alg-dispatch verifier accepting RS256 AND HS256
bypass_techniques: kid/jku header injection to point the verifier at attacker keys
alg:none / empty signature when the verifier also accepts it
crown_jewels: admin role claims overridden by token claims
treasury/admin endpoints gated only by a role claim

patterns.name: Web Cache Deception
patterns.signature: reverse-proxy caches static-extension URLs with a cookie-less cache key over a session-authenticated backend
references: Omer Gil — Web Cache Deception Attack
patterns.real_world: A reverse proxy caches static-extension URLs (.css/.js/.png) with a cache key that omits the session cookie, while a backend route (often a greedy regex like /account(/.*)?) serves per-session private data for those URLs. An attacker submits a victim-visited URL, the bot's private response is cached, then re-fetched anonymously.
detection_signatures: proxy_cache_key without $cookie over a session-authenticated backend
greedy backend route regex + static-extension passthrough
bypass_techniques: append a static extension to an authenticated path
path delimiters (; / ..) that still match the route regex
crown_jewels: api_key / session tokens in the cached body
any victim-session data cached under a static-extension URL

patterns.name: CORS Misconfiguration
patterns.signature: Access-Control-Allow-Origin reflects the request Origin (or is *) while credentials are allowed
references: PortSwigger — CORS vulnerability with basic origin reflection
patterns.real_world: A server echoes the request Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin while also sending Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Any website the victim visits can then make credentialed requests and read the victim's authenticated responses cross-origin (session theft, account data exfil).
bypass_techniques: subdomain of the attacker reflected by a naive suffix/prefix check
Origin with the target as a suffix (evil.com-target.com)

patterns.name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
patterns.signature: user-controlled input reaches a DOM/JS sink (innerHTML / dangerouslySetInnerHTML / document.write / .html / eval)
patterns.real_world: A DOM sink (innerHTML, document.write, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, jQuery .html(), eval) is fed user-controlled input without sanitization/encoding. The injected script runs in the victim's origin, stealing cookies, hijacking the session, or exfiltrating data.
detection_signatures: document.write(<var>) / .html(<var>) with a request/location source nearby
bypass_techniques: CSP bypass via nonce reuse / unsafe-inline gaps
crown_jewels: admin panel actions via CSRF tokens

patterns.name: Subdomain Takeover
patterns.signature: a DNS CNAME/AliasTarget points at a service that can be claimed by an attacker (GitHub Pages/S3/Heroku/…)
patterns.real_world: A dangling DNS record (CNAME/AliasTarget) points to a service the org no longer owns (e.g. a deleted GitHub Pages repo, S3 bucket, or Heroku app). An attacker re-registers that name and serves arbitrary content from the victim's subdomain — phishing, cookie theft via a parent-domain cookie, and same-origin attacks.
detection_signatures: aws_route53_record type=CNAME with an unclaimed service target
bypass_techniques: check the CNAME resolves to an NXDOMAIN / 'not found' / unclaimed page
verify via the service's provisioning page (GitHub 404 'repo not found')

patterns.name: OS Command Injection
patterns.real_world: User input is interpolated into a shell command (system/exec/popen/subprocess) without argument escaping. Attackers append ; | && $(...) to run arbitrary commands, from id/whoami probes to full reverse shells.
detection_signatures: raw input concatenated into a shell/exec sink
user-controlled parameter into os.system / subprocess / exec
bypass_techniques: $(...) and backtick substitution to bypass keyword filters
base64-encode the payload, then decode + execute
